question: How tall is the Burj Khalifa in meters?
raw_answer: The Burj Khalifa is 828 meters tall. This height is measured to the architectural top, including the spire, and is recognized as the world's tallest completed building by architectural height [5]. The spire contributes an additional 242.6 meters to the total height [3].

message.content: The Burj Khalifa is 828 meters tall. This height is measured to the architectural top, including the spire, and is recognized as the world's tallest completed building by architectural height [5]. The spire contributes an additional 242.6 meters to the total height [3].

passages.heading: Architecture and design
passages.text: The spire of Burj Khalifa is composed of more than 4,000 tonnes (4,400 short tons; 3,900 long tons) of structural steel. The central pinnacle pipe weighs 350 tonnes (390 short tons; 340 long tons) and has a height of 200 m (660 ft). The spire also houses communications equipment.<sup>[42]</sup> This 244-metre (801 ft) spire is widely considered vanity height, since very little of its space is usable. Without the spire, Burj Khalifa would be 585 metres (1,919 ft) tall. This was reported in a Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat study, which notes that the empty spire "could be a skyscraper on its own".<sup>[2]</sup> Such a skyscraper, if located in Europe, would be the 11th tallest building on that continent.<sup>[43]</sup>

passages.heading: Milestones
passages.text:
- 1 September 2008: Height tops 688 m (2,257 ft), making it the tallest human-made structure ever built, surpassing the previous record-holder, the Warsaw Radio Mast in Konstantynów, Poland.<sup>[110]</sup>
- 17 January 2009: Topped out at 829.8 m (2,722 ft).<sup>[111]</sup>
- 1 October 2009: Emaar announces that the exterior of the building is completed.<sup>[112]</sup>
- 4 January 2010: Burj Khalifa's official launch ceremony is held and Burj Khalifa is opened. Burj Dubai was renamed Burj Khalifa in honour of the President of the UAE and ruler of Abu Dhabi, Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed al Nahyan.<sup>[4]</sup>
- 10 March 2010: Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat certifies Burj Khalifa as world's tallest building.<sup>[113]</sup>

passages.heading: Awards
passages.text:
In June 2010, Burj Khalifa was the recipient of the 2010 "Best Tall Building Middle East & Africa" award by the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat.<sup>[158]</sup> On 28 September 2010 Burj Khalifa won the award for the best project of the year at the Middle East Architect Awards 2010.<sup>[159]</sup> Awards Chair Gordon Gill, of Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture, said:

We are talking about a building here that has changed the landscape of what is possible in architecture – a building that became internationally recognized as an icon long before it was even completed. 'Building of the Century' was thought a more apt title for it.<sup>[160]</sup>

passages.heading: How many world records does the Burj Khalifa hold?
passages.text: **Burj Khalifa**,  mixed-use skyscraper in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, that is the world’s tallest building, according to all three of the main criteria by which such buildings are judged (*see* Researcher’s Note: Heights of Buildings). Burj Khalifa (“Khalifa Tower”), known during construction as Burj Dubai, was officially named to honor the leader of the neighbouring emirate of Abu Dhabi, Sheikh Khalifa ibn Zayed Al Nahyan. Although the tower was formally opened on January 4, 2010, the entirety of the interior was not complete at that time. Built to house a variety of commercial, residential, and hospitality ventures, the tower—whose intended height remained a closely guarded secret throughout its construction—reached completion at 163 floors and a height of 2,717 feet (828 meters). It was designed by the Chicago-based architectural firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill. Adrian Smith served as architect, and William F. Baker served as structural engineer for this building.

passages.heading: How many world records does the Burj Khalifa hold?
passages.text: The building, modular in plan, is laid out on a three-lobed footprint that is an abstract rendering of the local *Hymenocallis* flower. The Y-shaped plan plays a central role in the reduction of wind forces on the tower. A hexagonal central core is buttressed by a series of wings, each with its own concrete core and perimeter columns. As the tower increases in height, the wings step back in a spiral configuration, changing the building’s shape at each tier and so reducing the effect of the wind on the building. The central core emerges at the tower’s top and is finished with a spire, which reaches more than 700 feet (200 meters). The spire was constructed inside the tower and hoisted to its final position using a hydraulic pump. At the foundational level, the tower is supported by a reinforced concrete mat nearly 13 feet (4 meters) thick, itself supported by concrete piles 5 feet (1.5 meters) in diameter. A three-story podium anchors the tower in place; the podium and two-story basement alone measure some 2,000,000 square feet (186,000 square meters) in their own right. The tower’s exterior cladding is made up of aluminum and stainless-steel panels, vertical stainless-steel tubular fins, and more than 28,000 hand-cut glass panels. A public observation deck, called “At the Top,” is located on the 124th floor.

passages.heading: How many world records does the Burj Khalifa hold?
passages.text: Upon its inauguration in January 2010, Burj Khalifa easily surpassed the Taipei 101 (Taipei Financial Center) building in Taipei, Taiwan, which measured 1,667 feet (508 meters), as the world’s tallest building. At the same time, Burj Khalifa broke numerous other records, including the world’s tallest freestanding structure, the world’s highest occupied floor, and the world’s highest outdoor observation deck.

passages.heading: Burj Al Khalifa: How Many Floors and Stories Does It Have?
passages.text: The Burj Khalifa’s highest floor accessible to the public is the 148th-floor observation deck at 555 meters. A second observation deck sits on the 124th floor at 452 meters. Above level 156, the structure transitions from concrete to steel, and the spire adds 242.6 meters to reach a total Burj Khalifa height in feet of 2,722 (829.8 meters to tip)—roughly three times the Eiffel Tower and nearly twice the Empire State Building.

passages.heading: Burj Khalifa View: Observation Decks and the Experience from the Top
passages.text: The experience of the tall Burj Khalifa is defined as much by movement as by form. The building contains 57 elevators, including double-deck units traveling at 10 meters per second, covering the longest elevator travel distance of any building at 504 meters. As cities grow vertically, architects must consider how such structures integrate into lived urban reality.

passages.heading: Burj Khalifa’s Legacy and the Future of Supertall Architecture
passages.text:
The Burj Khalifa occupies a complex position in architectural history—simultaneously an engineering marvel, a cultural symbol, and a subject of critical debate. Its significance extends beyond record-breaking height, offering insights into how architecture operates at the intersection of technology, identity, and urban ambition. Notably, the Jeddah Tower in Saudi Arabia—designed by the same architect, Adrian Smith—aims to surpass it as the first building to exceed 1,000 meters.

For contemporary practice, the Burj Khalifa demonstrates interdisciplinary collaboration, contextual sensitivity, and the ethical questions embedded in large-scale development. Its lesson is not that we can build higher, but that we must reassess why we build, for whom, and at what cost. The tower’s true legacy lies in the conversations it inspires within architectural culture.

passages.text: This is a list of the tallest buildings. Tall buildings, such as skyscrapers, are intended here as enclosed structures with continuously occupiable floors and a height of at least 350 metres (1,148 ft). Such definition excludes non-building structures, such as radio towers.

passages.heading: Ranking criteria and alternatives
passages.text: Until 1996, the world's tallest building was defined by the height to the top of the tallest architectural element, including spires but not antennae.<sup>[8]</sup> In 1930, this definitional argument led to a rivalry between the Bank of Manhattan Building and the Chrysler Building. The Bank of Manhattan Building (i.e. 40 Wall Street) employed only a short spire, was 282.5 m (927 ft) tall, and had a much higher top occupied floor (the second category in the 1996 criteria for tallest building). In contrast, the Chrysler Building employed a very large 38 m (125 ft) spire secretly assembled inside the building to claim the title of world's tallest building with a total height of 319 m (1046 ft), although it had a lower top occupied floor and a shorter height when both buildings' spires were excluded.<sup>[*citation needed*]</sup>

passages.heading: Height to roof
passages.text: This **list of tallest buildings by height to roof** ranks completed skyscrapers by height to roof which reach a height of 300 metres (984 ft) or more. Only buildings with continuously occupiable floors are included, thus non-building structures, including towers, are not included. Some assessments of the tallest building use 'height to roof' to determine tallest building, as 'architectural feature' is regarded as a subjective and an imprecise comparative measure. However, in November 2009, the CTBUH stopped using the roof height as the metric for tall buildings because modern tall buildings rarely have a part of the building that can categorically be deemed the roof.<sup>[115]</sup>

828 metres tall, Burj Khalifa is a mixed-use skyscraper in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. It ranks first among the world's tallest completed buildings by architectural height. [2]

INSIDE THE ENGINEERING

How Burj Khalifa was built.

Design, structure and construction. Technical sources reviewed 9 September 2026.

SOM arranged three concrete wings around a six-sided core. Each wing braces the other two, while the central cell supplies torsional stiffness. The setback geometry aligns columns above with walls below, avoiding disruptive transfers as the floor plate reduces. Gravity and lateral resistance follow the same disciplined geometry.

A reinforced-concrete mat, 3.7 metres thick, distributes the tower load to bored piles 1.5 metres in diameter and 43 metres long. The mat was cast in four pours totalling 12,500 cubic metres. Low-permeability concrete forms part of the foundation durability strategy.

The Samsung C&T, Six Construct and Arabtec joint venture had to coordinate cranes, labour and material supply vertically. BESIX reports concrete pumping to 585 metres and cycles reaching two floors per week. Special mixes and predominantly night-time pours addressed temperatures exceeding 45°C.

Successive setbacks change the shape the wind encounters, reducing coherent vortex formation. The envelope uses silver-coated glazing to limit solar gain. Mechanical equipment is distributed through double-height service floors; the design also collects air-conditioning condensate for reuse. The steel spire was assembled inside the building and hydraulically raised into position.
